note.front: What does HTML stand for, and what is its primary purpose?
note.back: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It describes the structure and meaning of web content; CSS presents it and JavaScript adds behavior.

note.front: How do HTML, CSS, and JavaScript differ?
note.back: HTML provides content and structure, CSS controls presentation and layout, and JavaScript provides scripting and dynamic behavior.

note.front: What is the purpose of <!DOCTYPE html>?
note.back: It tells the browser to use standards mode for the document. In HTML5, the declaration is short and case-insensitive; it is not an HTML element.

note.front: What is the role of the <html> element?
note.back: It is the root element containing the whole document, including <head> and <body>. Its lang attribute should identify the document language.

note.front: What belongs in an HTML document's <head>?
note.back: Metadata and resources for the document, such as <title>, <meta>, stylesheets, scripts, icons, and preload hints. Visible page content belongs in <body>.

note.front: What belongs inside <body>?
note.back: The document content rendered in the page: headings, paragraphs, links, images, forms, lists, tables, and other visible or interactive elements.

note.front: Why should the root element include a lang attribute?
note.back: It tells browsers and assistive technologies the language of the content, improving pronunciation, translation, and accessibility. Example: <html lang="en">.

note.front: What does <meta charset="UTF-8"> do?
note.back: It declares the document's character encoding as UTF-8, allowing a broad range of characters to be interpreted correctly. It should appear near the beginning of <head>.

note.front: What is the purpose of the viewport meta tag?
note.back: It controls the layout viewport on mobile devices. The common value width=device-width, initial-scale=1 makes the CSS viewport match the device width and starts at normal zoom.

note.front: What does the <title> element provide?
note.back: The document title shown in the browser tab, bookmarks, history, and often search results. Each document should have one descriptive <title> in its <head>.

note.front: What is the purpose of <meta name="description">?
note.back: It supplies a short description of the page that search engines may use in result snippets. It does not directly determine the page's ranking.

note.front: How do you write an HTML comment?
note.back: Use <!-- comment text -->. Comments are ignored by the browser when rendering, but they remain visible in the source.

note.front: What is an HTML element?
note.back:
An element is a complete piece of markup, usually consisting of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag, such as

Text

. Some elements are void and have no closing tag.

note.front: What is the difference between a tag and an HTML element?
note.back:
A tag is the markup delimiter such as

or

; an element includes the tags plus its content and children.

note.front: What is an HTML attribute?
note.back: An attribute supplies extra information or configuration on an element's opening tag, for example href on an anchor or alt on an image. Most values use quotes.

note.front: What is a boolean attribute?
note.back: A boolean attribute represents true by being present and false by being absent. Its value is not normally needed; for example, <input required> means the control is required.

note.front: What are global HTML attributes?
note.back: Attributes usable on most or all HTML elements, including id, class, title, hidden, lang, dir, and data-*.

note.front: What makes an HTML id value valid and useful?
note.back: An id uniquely identifies an element within the document. It must not contain spaces; it can be targeted by fragment links, CSS, JavaScript, and accessibility relationships.

note.front: What is the purpose of the class attribute?
note.back: It assigns one or more space-separated class names to an element. Classes are reusable hooks for CSS and JavaScript, unlike an id, which should be unique.

note.front: What are data-* attributes used for?
note.back: They store custom, non-visible data on standard HTML elements without inventing invalid attributes. JavaScript can read them through element.dataset; for example, data-user-id maps to dataset.userId.

note.front: What does the hidden attribute do?
note.back: It marks an element as not currently relevant for presentation. User agents generally hide it, but it is not a security mechanism; CSS or JavaScript can reveal the element.

note.front: What are <h1> through <h6> used for?
note.back: They are six levels of section headings, from highest importance (<h1>) to lowest (<h6>). Choose the level based on document structure, not visual size.

note.front: What is a good rule for heading hierarchy?
note.back: Use headings in a logical outline: a page normally has one primary <h1>, followed by nested <h2> and <h3> sections as needed. Do not skip levels merely to change font size.

note.front:
What does the

element represent?
note.back: A paragraph of prose. Browsers normally render paragraphs as block-level content with spacing between them; use CSS for that spacing rather than empty paragraphs.

note.front:
When should
be used?
note.back:
Use it for a meaningful line break within phrasing content, such as a postal address or poem. Do not use repeated
elements for layout; use CSS instead.

note.front: What does <hr> represent semantically?
note.back: A thematic break between paragraphs or sections, such as a change of topic. Its visual line is only a default presentation that CSS can change.

note.front: What is the difference between <strong> and <b>?
note.back: <strong> conveys strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. <b> draws attention without adding importance. Both may appear bold by default, but meaning should guide the choice.

note.front: What is the difference between <em> and <i>?
note.back: <em> marks stress emphasis that can change a sentence's meaning. <i> marks text set apart from normal prose, such as a term, idiom, or taxonomic name, without stress emphasis.

note.front: What does the <mark> element mean?
note.back: It marks text as relevant or highlighted in the current context, such as search-result matches. Its default yellow background is presentation, not the meaning itself.

note.front: What is the purpose of <small>?
note.back: It represents side comments, small print, or fine print such as copyright and legal text. It does not make arbitrary text more important or provide a reliable accessibility label.

note.front: How do <del> and <ins> represent document edits?
note.back: <del> represents content that was removed, while <ins> represents content that was added. Optional datetime attributes can record when the change occurred.

note.front: What are <sub> and <sup> for?
note.back: <sub> marks subscript text, such as the 2 in H2O. <sup> marks superscript text, such as an exponent or footnote marker. They are semantic, not general positioning tools.

note.front: How should a long quotation be marked up?
note.back: Use <blockquote> for a quotation from another source. A cite attribute may contain the source URL, while a visible source can be marked with <cite>.

note.front: When should <q> be used instead of <blockquote>?
note.back: Use <q> for a short inline quotation and <blockquote> for a standalone, longer quotation. Browsers may add quotation marks around <q> automatically.

note.front: What does <abbr title="..."> provide?
note.back: <abbr> identifies an abbreviation or acronym. The title attribute can provide its expanded form, though important expansions should also be understandable from visible content.

note.front: What is the purpose of the <time> element?
note.back: It represents a date, time, duration, or machine-readable timestamp. Use datetime for a parseable value, for example <time datetime="2025-01-01">New Year's Day</time>.

note.front: Which element marks a short fragment of computer code?
note.back: Use <code> for a short inline fragment, such as npm install. It conveys code semantics; the browser's monospace styling is only a default.

note.front: What is <pre> used for?
note.back:
It represents preformatted text where whitespace and line breaks are significant. It is commonly combined with for multi-line source code: 
...
.

note.front: What do <kbd>, <samp>, and <var> represent?
note.back: <kbd> marks user input such as a key, <samp> marks sample output from a program, and <var> marks a variable or placeholder.

note.front: How do you write a literal less-than sign in HTML text?
note.back: Use the character reference <. Likewise, use > for a greater-than sign when needed and & for an ampersand that must not begin a character reference.

note.front: How does HTML normally treat consecutive spaces and line breaks in text?
note.back: Normal HTML rendering collapses runs of whitespace into a single space. Use semantic elements, CSS such as white-space, or <pre> when whitespace must be preserved.

note.front: What does the <a> element create?
note.back: It creates a hyperlink when it has an href destination. The linked text should describe the destination or action, rather than saying only “click here.”

note.front: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative URL?
note.back: An absolute URL includes the scheme and host, such as https://example.com/docs. A relative URL is resolved from the current document or base URL, such as ../docs or /docs.

note.front: How do you link to a location within the current page?
note.back: Give the destination element a unique id, then use a fragment URL such as href="#contact". The browser scrolls to the element with id="contact".

note.front: What should usually accompany target="_blank"?
note.back: Use rel="noopener" to prevent the new page from controlling the opener through window.opener. Modern browsers often imply noopener, but stating it explicitly is clear; add noreferrer only when its referrer behavior is wanted.

note.front: How can an anchor start an email or telephone action?
note.back: Use a scheme in href: mailto:person@example.com for email or tel:+15551234567 for telephone links. The device decides which application handles the scheme.

note.front: Which element embeds an image, and which attributes are essential?
note.back: Use . src identifies the image resource and alt provides its text alternative. img is a void element.

note.front: How should the alt value differ for informative and decorative images?
note.back: For an informative image, describe its relevant purpose or content. For a purely decorative image, use alt="" so assistive technology can skip it. Do not repeat nearby visible text unnecessarily.

note.front: When should <figure> and <figcaption> be used?
note.back: Use <figure> for self-contained content such as an image, diagram, code sample, or quote that can be moved away from the main flow. Put its visible caption in <figcaption>.

note.front: What problem does <picture> solve?
note.back: It provides art direction or alternative image sources selected by media conditions, with a fallback . Use it when different crops or formats are needed, not merely to list resolutions.

note.front: What are srcset and sizes used for on images?
note.back: srcset lists candidate image resources, commonly with width or pixel-density descriptors. sizes tells the browser the rendered width under viewport conditions so it can choose an efficient candidate.

note.front: What does loading="lazy" do on an image or iframe?
note.back: It hints that the browser may defer loading the resource until it is near the viewport. It can improve initial performance, but it is only a hint and should not be used for critical above-the-fold content.

note.front: How do you embed audio with HTML?
note.back: Use <audio controls> with one or more <source src="..." type="..."> elements and fallback text. The controls attribute displays the browser's playback controls.

note.front: How do you embed video with HTML?
note.back: Use <video controls>, optionally with width, poster, and multiple <source> elements. Include fallback text and provide captions when dialogue or important audio is present.

note.front: What is the purpose of <track kind="captions">?
note.back: It associates a timed text file, usually WebVTT, with audio or video. Captions make spoken dialogue and meaningful sounds available to deaf or hard-of-hearing users.

note.front: What does an <iframe> do, and what security control is commonly useful?
note.back: It embeds another browsing context, such as another page or an external widget. Use the sandbox attribute to restrict capabilities, and grant only needed exceptions with sandbox tokens.

note.front: When should you use <ul>?
note.back: Use an unordered list when the order of the items is not meaningful. Each direct child item should normally be an <li>.

note.front: When should you use <ol>?
note.back: Use an ordered list when sequence or ranking matters, such as steps in a procedure. Its start, reversed, and type attributes can adjust numbering semantics.

note.front: What are <dl>, <dt>, and <dd> for?
note.back: They represent a description list: <dt> contains a term or name and <dd> contains its description or value. They can represent glossaries, metadata, or question-and-answer pairs.

note.front: How do you create a nested list?
note.back: Place the nested <ul> or <ol> inside the parent list item's <li>, after the parent item's text. Do not make the nested list a direct child of the outer list beside an <li>.

note.front: When is the <table> element appropriate?
note.back: Use it for two-dimensional tabular data where rows and columns have relationships. Do not use tables solely for page layout; use CSS layout systems instead.

note.front: What does <caption> provide for a table?
note.back: A visible title or brief explanation of the table's purpose. It should be the first child of <table> and helps users decide whether the table is relevant.

note.front: What are <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> used for?
note.back: They group table header rows, body rows, and footer or summary rows. The groups improve structure and can help styling and accessibility; <tbody> is commonly used for the main data.

note.front: What is the difference between <th> and <td>?
note.back: <th> is a header cell that labels a row or column, while <td> is a data cell. Header cells carry semantic relationships that ordinary bold text does not.

note.front: What does the scope attribute on a table header communicate?
note.back: It identifies which cells a header applies to. Common values are col, row, colgroup, and rowgroup; this helps assistive technologies associate headers with data.

note.front: What do colspan and rowspan do?
note.back: colspan makes a cell span multiple columns, while rowspan makes it span multiple rows. Their numeric values change the table's grid and must match the intended structure.

note.front: How can a complex table associate headers with data cells?
note.back: Give headers unique id values and put a space-separated list of those IDs in each data cell's headers attribute. For simpler tables, scope is usually preferable.

note.front: Why should CSS, rather than HTML tables, handle page layout?
note.back: Tables express data relationships and impose a tabular accessibility structure. Using them for layout makes responsive design and navigation harder and can mislead assistive technology users.

note.front: What is semantic HTML?
note.back: Semantic HTML uses elements according to their meaning and purpose, such as <nav> for navigation and <button> for an action. It improves accessibility, maintainability, and machine understanding.

note.front: What content commonly belongs in <header>?
note.back: Introductory content for a page or section, such as a heading, logo, author information, or navigation. A document can have multiple headers when sections or articles need their own introductions.

note.front: What is <nav> for?
note.back: It marks a major block of navigation links, such as a primary menu, table of contents, or pagination. Not every group of links needs to be inside <nav>.

note.front: What is the purpose of <main>?
note.back: It contains the dominant, unique content of the document. There should normally be one visible <main> per page, excluding repeated navigation, headers, and footers.

note.front: When should content be an <article>?
note.back: Use <article> for a self-contained composition that could be distributed or understood independently, such as a post, news story, comment, or product card.

note.front: When should content be a <section>?
note.back: Use <section> for a thematic grouping of content, usually with a heading. Do not use it as a generic styling wrapper when <div> is more accurate.

note.front: What does <aside> represent?
note.back: Content tangentially related to its surrounding content, such as a sidebar, related links, pull quote, or glossary. It is not simply a synonym for any content placed on the side visually.

note.front: What is the role of <footer>?
note.back: It contains footer information for its nearest sectioning content or the page, such as author details, copyright, related links, or navigation. A page and its articles can each have a footer.

note.front: When should you use <div>?
note.back: Use <div> as a generic block container when no more meaningful semantic element fits. It has no inherent meaning and should not replace headings, buttons, links, or landmarks.

note.front: What is the purpose of <span>?
note.back: It is a generic inline container with no inherent meaning, useful for styling or scripting a run of phrasing content when a semantic inline element does not apply.

note.front: What do <details> and <summary> provide?
note.back: They create a native disclosure widget. <summary> is the always-visible label; the remaining content can be expanded or collapsed. Add open when it should start expanded.

note.front: What is the purpose of the <form> element?
note.back: It groups interactive controls for submitting user-entered data. Its action identifies the submission destination and its method selects how the data is sent.

note.front: What does a form's action attribute specify?
note.back: It specifies the URL that receives the submitted form data. If omitted, the browser submits to the document's current URL, subject to the form and document context.

note.front: What are the main differences between form methods GET and POST?
note.back: GET appends the encoded data to the URL, making it useful for safe, bookmarkable queries. POST sends data in the request body and is preferred for actions or larger/sensitive payloads, but HTTPS is still required for confidentiality.

note.front: How should a text input be associated with its label?
note.back: Give the control an id and set the label's for attribute to the same value, or wrap the control inside <label>. A label makes the control easier to understand and enlarges its click target.

note.front: What are useful HTML <input> types?
note.back: Examples include text, email, password, number, date, url, search, tel, checkbox, radio, file, and hidden. The type enables appropriate semantics, validation, and user-interface hints.

note.front: Why is the name attribute important on a form control?
note.back: It supplies the key used when the control's successful value is included in form submission. A control without a name generally contributes no named form data.

note.front: What does an input's value attribute represent?
note.back: It provides the control's initial value and, for many controls, the value submitted when selected or changed. For checkboxes and radio buttons, it is the submitted value when that control is checked.

note.front: What does the required attribute do?
note.back: It makes a supported form control fail native constraint validation when it has no value. It provides client-side guidance, not server-side security; the server must validate submitted data too.

note.front: Why should a placeholder not replace a label?
note.back: A placeholder disappears when the user types, can have low contrast, and is not a durable name for the control. Provide a visible <label>; use placeholder only for an optional format or example.

note.front: What does the autocomplete attribute control?
note.back: It tells the browser what kind of value a control or form expects and whether saved values may be suggested. Tokens such as email, name, and shipping postal-code help browsers fill forms accurately.

note.front: How do <select> and <option> work together?
note.back: <select> creates a selection control and its <option> children represent choices. The selected option's value (or its text when no value is provided) is submitted under the select's name.

note.front: What is <textarea> used for?
note.back: It creates a multi-line text input. Its initial value is the text between the opening and closing tags, not a value attribute; rows and cols provide initial size hints.

note.front: What are the default button types, and which type is safest for a non-submit action inside a form?
note.back: A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit". Use type="button" for actions such as opening a dialog or changing a preview when submission is not intended; use type="reset" only deliberately.

note.front: What do <fieldset> and <legend> provide?
note.back: <fieldset> groups related form controls, and its first <legend> labels the group. This is especially useful for radio-button sets and checkbox groups.

note.front: How does a checkbox differ from a radio button?
note.back: A checkbox represents an independent on/off choice and multiple checkboxes can be selected. Radio buttons form a mutually exclusive group when they share the same name; normally exactly one is selected for a required choice.

note.front: What is the difference between disabled and readonly?
note.back: A disabled control cannot be focused or edited and is not submitted. A readonly text-like control cannot be edited but can usually be focused and submitted; neither replaces server-side authorization checks.

note.front: What do min, max, and step constrain?
note.back: For supported numeric, date, and time controls, min and max define bounds and step defines valid increments. They participate in native constraint validation.

note.front: What does the pattern attribute do?
note.back: It supplies a regular-expression constraint for supported text-like inputs. The entire value must conform for validity; use a label and helpful instructions as well, because a pattern alone does not explain the expected format.

note.front: What are <datalist> and an input's list attribute for?
note.back: <datalist> provides suggested values for an input. Set the input's list attribute to the datalist's id. Suggestions do not necessarily restrict the user to those values.

note.front: What is ARIA, and what rule should guide its use?
note.back: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds roles, states, and properties when native HTML cannot express the needed accessibility semantics. Prefer semantic native elements first: do not use ARIA to recreate a native button, link, or form control unnecessarily.

note.front: What does tabindex control, and which values should generally be avoided?
note.back: It controls whether and where an element participates in sequential keyboard focus. Avoid positive values such as tabindex="1", which create a brittle custom order; use native interactive elements and usually tabindex="0" or -1 only for specific focus-management needs.
